title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law: Impact, Opportunities, and Risks
pub: Minnesota Journal of Law, Science & Technology, vol. 25, no. 2, pp. 25-48 (2024)
author: John Villasenor

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: Villasenor acknowledges uneven augmentation outcomes and calls for safeguards in public-facing legal AI, but he does not directly assess whether human oversight provides effective control, requires independent verification, or preserves the expertise needed for judgment. His principal focus is instead the predicted transformation of legal writing and barriers to access-to-justice deployment.

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The source endorses supervised curricular use of generative AI rather than prohibition while preserving student authorship, independent verification and responsibility for submitted work. Its emphasis on substantive editing so outputs reflect students’ own thinking aligns directly with the cluster’s distinction between AI-assisted performance and intellectual development, though it offers recommendations rather than empirical evidence of learning gains.
qs: Law schools should view generative AI as an opportunity as opposed to a threat.56 Rather than banning student use of ChatGPT for assignments, they should help students learn how to use generative AI tools, while also instructing them on their appropriate use.
This includes independently checking citations and assertions of fact for accuracy and running the output of a generative AI system through a plagiarism checker to see if there are any matches.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source supports integrating AI competence with independent legal judgment rather than imposing broad bans. It advocates responsible AI-assisted writing, student accountability, independent verification and substantive editing, while acknowledging uneven empirical benefits and leaving exam policy unresolved. Its objections to unreliable detection-based enforcement also align with the cluster’s preference for assessment rules that distinguish unaided competence from responsible AI-assisted work.
qs: Law schools should view generative AI as an opportunity as opposed to a threat.56 Rather than banning student use of ChatGPT for assignments, they should help students learn how to use generative AI tools, while also instructing them on their appropriate use.
Students should be told that they are fully accountable for any writing that they turn in listing them as an author.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: Villasenor supports the cluster’s core account: generative AI can produce substantive legal drafts and improve selected tasks, but its usefulness is task-dependent and requires users to understand its limitations. His claims about broader transformation and access are prospective, and the supplied evidence does not specifically develop the cluster’s stronger requirements for lawyer verification, supervision and responsibility.
qs: It can be used to accelerate legal research and to produce drafts of text for use in contracts, regulatory filings, court rulings, academic papers, wills, trusts, patent specifications, affidavits, articles of incorporation, and more.
In short, generative AI is an extraordinarily powerful tool, but as with any tool, using it effectively requires an understanding of its strengths as well as of its shortcomings and limitations.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source supports the distinction between mere AI access and professional readiness. It advocates structured instruction in responsible use while requiring students to retain authorship responsibility, independently verify citations and facts, and substantively edit outputs. Its recognition of uneven exam gains and uncertainty about future tools also aligns with the cluster’s caution that short-term performance does not establish durable competence.
qs: To be most effective in helping students develop that proficiency, law schools should update their legal research and writing instruction to specifically teach students the skills to responsibly use generative AI.
This includes independently checking citations and assertions of fact for accuracy and running the output of a generative AI system through a plagiarism checker to see if there are any matches.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: Villasenor supports the cluster’s calibrated position: AI may expand provider capacity and lower access barriers, but public-facing uses should not be fully automated and require human review, adequate quality, privacy protection and regulatory safeguards. His account is more prospective and gives less attention to users’ limited verification capacity, unequal risk distribution and the distinction between access to filing and access to effective remedies.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core rejection of both blanket bans and unrestricted assistance: it advocates teaching appropriate AI use while holding students accountable for verifying and editing outputs. It does not, however, specifically develop the cluster’s stage-based sequencing of unaided foundational work followed by supervised AI practice.
qs: Law schools should view generative AI as an opportunity as opposed to a threat.56 Rather than banning student use of ChatGPT for assignments, they should help students learn how to use generative AI tools, while also instructing them on their appropriate use.
This includes independently checking citations and assertions of fact for accuracy and running the output of a generative AI system through a plagiarism checker to see if there are any matches.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: Villasenor supports the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI may lower barriers to legal services, but that access gains require gradual regulatory adaptation, consumer protection and continued human judgment. His emphasis on selective use, verification and education also aligns with the cluster’s preference for guarded assistance over either prohibition or autonomous substitution.
qs: category of generative AI systems, and updating regulatory frameworks to permit their deployment while ensuring appropriate levels of consumer protection will take years.45 But in the not-too-distant future, it seems reasonable to expect that generative AI will become a key mechanism for lowering the barriers to obtaining legal services.

In a world where high performance generative AI tools are common, the most effective attorneys will not be those who use AI the most, but rather will be those who use it judiciously and carefully while also knowing when not to use it.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s copilot framing and selective, task-specific adoption: it predicts efficiency gains for some research and writing tasks while reserving contextual reasoning, advocacy and judgment for lawyers. It does not materially develop the cluster’s central analysis of verification costs, grounding limits or measured quality evidence.
qs: It argues that for some legal research and writing tasks, generative AI will lead to considerable efficiency improvements.

In a world where high performance generative AI tools are common, the most effective attorneys will not be those who use AI the most, but rather will be those who use it judiciously and carefully while also knowing when not to use it.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that legal GenAI can assist drafting while accuracy checks remain necessary. Its forecasts that automated verification will improve reliability and produce large time savings are prospective rather than empirical, so they illustrate the cluster’s optimistic side without showing that residual errors or human verification costs have been eliminated.
qs: Companies making AI systems for drafting legal filings will presumably include a feature that automatically runs system outputs through verification to ensure that all citations and other assertions of fact are accurate.
Using this process, the attorney may be able to produce in an afternoon a document that without AI would have required multiple days of drafting and revising.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Villasenor aligns closely with the cluster: he finds substantial but task-bounded efficiency gains, distinguishes fluent production from legal judgment, requires verification and substantive human revision, and recommends selective adoption supported by training, confidentiality safeguards and ongoing support. His optimism about future quality and access is more affirmative than the synthesis, but remains qualified and does not amount to disagreement.
qs: a paper describing the results of “the first randomized controlled trial of AI assistance’s effect on human legal analysis,” Choi, Monahan, and Schwarcz “found that access to GPT-4 slightly and inconsistently improved the quality of participants’ legal analysis but induced large and consistent increases in speed.”27  IEEE TECH.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source broadly supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition by recognising that some tasks are unsuitable for generative AI and that adoption requires systems combining output quality, flexibility and usability. However, it gives little attention to substantive verification or task-specific evaluation and presents significant efficiency gains as an expectation rather than a demonstrated result.
qs: It also considers tasks not well suited to generative AI.

One of the tasks for designers of these systems will be to ensure that they have the flexibility and capacity to produce high- quality outputs while also being sufficiently user-friendly to enable broad adoption.

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: The source aligns with selective delegation by predicting efficiency gains for some research and writing tasks while expecting little assistance with reasoning and highly fact- or case-specific analysis. It presents these as longer-term arguments rather than empirical proof of reliable performance or net productivity.
qs: It argues that for some legal research and writing tasks, generative AI will lead to considerable efficiency improvements.
It also argues that there are aspects of legal writing—including reasoning and performing highly fact- and case-specific detailed analysis— where generative AI will offer little help.

st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: Villasenor supports the cluster’s central distinction between cheap, rapid legal-text production and effective legal assistance: the cited experiment shows stronger speed than quality gains, and he maintains that contextual legal judgment remains necessary. He presents expanded access as prospective rather than demonstrated, but does not examine rising self-representation or shifted costs to courts and opponents.
qs: a paper describing the results of “the first randomized controlled trial of AI assistance’s effect on human legal analysis,” Choi, Monahan, and Schwarcz “found that access to GPT-4 slightly and inconsistently improved the quality of participants’ legal analysis but induced large and consistent increases in speed.”27  IEEE TECH.
Generative AI makes it easy to produce text, but that does not mean that the resulting text will optimally advance and support an argument.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Villasenor aligns with the cluster’s copilot model: AI can accelerate legal work, but lawyers and students must use it selectively, retain substantive judgment, and independently verify outputs. He also supports institutional testing, confidentiality review, training, and gradual adoption, though he does not directly establish that verification will consume most efficiency gains.
qs: In a world where high performance generative AI tools are common, the most effective attorneys will not be those who use AI the most, but rather will be those who use it judiciously and carefully while also knowing when not to use it.
This includes independently checking citations and assertions of fact for accuracy and running the output of a generative AI system through a plagiarism checker to see if there are any matches.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core augmentation account: generative AI can improve selected legal tasks while important responsibilities remain human. It also treats broader access and educational adaptation as possibilities or recommendations rather than established outcomes. It does not materially address how this complementarity may reshape staffing or business models.
qs: It argues that for some legal research and writing tasks, generative AI will lead to considerable efficiency improvements.
But as powerful as generative AI is, it is not now—and will not in the future ever become—a replacement for some of the most important tasks that attorneys do.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Villasenor closely supports the cluster’s principal proposition: generative AI offers substantial efficiency gains on selected legal tasks but limited help with fact-specific reasoning, so deployment should remain human-led, usable and subject to verification rather than treated as general legal autonomy. His motion-drafting and supervised access-to-justice examples reinforce work redesign around initial drafts, lawyer judgment and review.

Even allowing for five, ten, or fifteen years of technological advances, that draft will not be perfect, and will need wordsmithing and fact checking.

kp.k: Generative AI changes argument production, not merely information retrieval
kp.d: Villasenor argues that generative AI differs from earlier legal technologies because it contributes directly to articulating arguments. He contrasts this with digitization, electronic discovery and search, whose effects partly offset one another as search capabilities expanded alongside information volumes. He predicts gradual but profound changes in legal writing, client expectations, service access and education, while explicitly cautioning that technological forecasts are uncertain.
qs: Unlike the technologies described above, which were designed to help attorneys efficiently find information that they could then use in formulating and supporting arguments, generative AI can directly contribute to the process of articulating arguments.
Before proceeding, it is important to underscore that any attempt to predict the future impact of a technology is fraught.

kp.k: Early experimental evidence supports speed more consistently than quality
kp.d: The article reports Choi, Monahan and Schwarcz’s randomized controlled trial of AI assistance in human legal analysis, rather than presenting original experimental findings. The cited result is that GPT-4 access produced large, consistent speed improvements but only slight, inconsistent improvements in analytical quality. Villasenor uses this as early evidence supporting efficiency gains across research and document drafting.
qs: the first randomized controlled trial of AI assistance’s effect on human legal analysis
found that access to GPT-4 slightly and inconsistently improved the quality of participants’ legal analysis but induced large and consistent increases in speed.

kp.k: Future motion drafting remains attorney-directed and human-checked
kp.d: In an explicitly hypothetical scenario five, ten or fifteen years ahead, attorneys identify the strongest arguments and supply case materials, authorities, comparable filings and formatting constraints; AI then produces initial drafts. Villasenor suggests that this could compress several days of drafting into an afternoon, but requires fact checking and revision. Reduced hallucinations and automatic citation and factual checking are predictions, not demonstrated capabilities.
qs: First, think not of today’s generative AI technology, but rather the technology that will be available in five, ten, or fifteen years.
Identifying these key arguments is a core intellectual contribution that the attorney is providing, and it has very little to do with AI.
Even allowing for five, ten, or fifteen years of technological advances, that draft will not be perfect, and will need wordsmithing and fact checking.
Using this process, the attorney may be able to produce in an afternoon a document that without AI would have required multiple days of drafting and revising.

kp.k: AI enables alternative drafts, revision and adversarial preparation
kp.d: Villasenor proposes generating multiple independent drafts and manually combining their best elements, exploiting variation in model outputs at essentially no additional generation time or cost. Other suggested applications include expanding rough drafts, adding citations, improving concision and persuasiveness, identifying potential rebuttals, detecting inconsistencies with earlier filings and finding cases persuasive to the relevant courts.
qs: Randomness can similarly be leveraged in future generative AI systems to generate two or three drafts of a document.
Yet another option would be to use AI to revise arguments to present them more convincingly or concisely, or to identify potential rebuttals that the attorney might want to address.
AI could also be used to find apparent or actual inconsistencies with statements made in earlier filings.

kp.k: Strategic judgment and relationships remain central human contributions
kp.d: The author argues that selecting decisive case details and weighing client goals, budgets, risk tolerance, witnesses and litigation strengths require attorneys’ contextual understanding. His broader conclusion is a categorical prediction that AI will never replace some central professional activities, including client relationships, strategic advice, mentoring and responding dynamically in proceedings; this is his argument, not an empirical finding.
qs: In a world where high performance generative AI tools are common, the most effective attorneys will not be those who use AI the most, but rather will be those who use it judiciously and carefully while also knowing when not to use it.
A good attorney will know the goals, budget, and risk tolerance of the client, the strengths and weaknesses of the parties’ arguments, the anticipated effectiveness of trial witnesses, and much more.
But as powerful as generative AI is, it is not now—and will not in the future ever become—a replacement for some of the most important tasks that attorneys do.

kp.k: Tenant assistance illustrates potential justice-gap reduction
kp.d: Drawing on the Legal Services Corporation’s 2022 Justice Gap Survey, based on a survey conducted in 2021, Villasenor reports that 74% of low-income households experienced at least one civil legal problem in the preceding year and that 55% of low-income Americans personally experiencing a problem said it substantially affected their lives. He proposes multilingual, interactive AI assistance that collects tenants’ accounts and documentation, requests clarifications, drafts harassment-claim forms and allows tenant review before generating filing documents. These workflows are prospective; the cited New York tenant-risk identification work used machine learning without mentioning generative AI.
qs: 74% of “low-income households experienced 1+ civil legal problems in the past year,”
55% of “low-income Americans who personally experienced a problem say these problems substantially impacted their lives.”
The system could be highly interactive and available in multiple languages.
It could then prompt the tenant to either approve the forms, or to identify and revise any portions that need revision.

kp.k: Legal-services organizations could expand capacity through supervised AI
kp.d: The article proposes customized internal tools for city governments and private legal-services organizations to draft claims and pre-claim letters to landlords. A hybrid model would let tenants enter information before staff review and amend AI-generated documents. Villasenor predicts broader service coverage by experienced staff, expressly rejecting fully automated use because fact patterns vary too much.
qs: Such systems will not be used in a fully automated, push- button manner, as there is far too much variation in the fact patterns involved.
Once draft documents are created by a generative AI system based on the tenants’ input, staff members at the tenants’ rights organization can review them, making any necessary changes.

kp.k: Quality, privacy and legal restrictions condition justice applications
kp.d: Villasenor warns that premature deployment could generate poor filings, frustrate users and undermine subsequent adoption. Systems must protect personally identifiable information and address privacy and privilege implications. Citing unauthorized-practice litigation against LegalZoom as an analogy, he anticipates litigation against automated pro se assistance and expects development, testing, litigation and consumer-protective regulatory adaptation to take years. Arizona and Utah reforms are cited as examples of regulatory change, not as AI-specific measures.
qs: Another issue is that by definition, such a system would need to collect personally identifiable information and other information with privacy and privilege implications.
For AI solutions for pro se litigants, the act of providing assistance using a generative AI system would itself spur litigation.

Performing the requisite software development and testing, navigating the litigation that may accompany releases of products in this category of generative AI systems, and updating regulatory frameworks to permit their deployment while ensuring appropriate levels of consumer protection will take years.

kp.k: Firm adoption requires balancing competitiveness against early-adopter costs
kp.d: The author predicts that firms ignoring AI will eventually face higher delivery costs than competitors, but cautions that early products may be expensive, training-intensive, immature or commercially short-lived. He recommends proportionate engagement: larger firms could establish committees to test tools for workflow benefits, manageable training requirements, confidentiality and market durability, followed by training and ongoing support. Ease of use is presented as a central adoption condition, drawing an analogy with web browsers and Internet growth.
qs: Over the long term, firms that fail to take advantage of those efficiency advantages will incur more costs relative to their competitors in delivering services.
Not all law firms will want to take on the burden that accompanies being an early adopter.
Once a tool is made available firm- wide, the firm will also need to facilitate training opportunities for the firm’s attorneys as well as ensure that they have access to ongoing support.
It will be important for law firms to observe market dynamics, and to recognize that the early generative AI market leaders may not stay in that position.

kp.k: Law schools should teach responsible AI use
kp.d: Villasenor recommends updating legal research and writing instruction and permitting responsible AI use in paper assignments, including outside dedicated writing courses. Students should learn prompting, substantive editing, independent citation and factual checking, and plagiarism checking while retaining full accountability. He predicts that proficiency will improve graduates’ efficiency and employment prospects, but cautions schools about vendor incentives to obtain student testing data and institutional prestige through early adoption. The article does not prescribe when AI should be permitted in examinations.
qs: Law schools should prepare students for the technology environment they will inhabit, as opposed to the technology environment their teachers may view as most familiar.
Students should be told that they are fully accountable for any writing that they turn in listing them as an author.
This includes independently checking citations and assertions of fact for accuracy and running the output of a generative AI system through a plagiarism checker to see if there are any matches.

kp.k: Reported student outcomes reveal uneven benefits from AI assistance
kp.d: The article reports Choi and Schwarcz’s study of AI assistance on law-school examinations: consistent benefits occurred only on simple multiple-choice questions, and effectively prompted GPT-4 alone outperformed students both with and without assistance. Lower-performing students gained most, while higher-performing students experienced declines. Villasenor suggests that limited student experience and immature tools explain these results, and predicts improvement with better tools and skills; those explanations and expectations are not themselves reported experimental findings.
qs: found that students consistently benefited from AI assistance only on simple multiple-choice questions and that GPT-4 alone outperformed both students alone and students with AI assistance with effective prompt engineering.
large variation in the effect of AI assistance, with the worst- performing students seeing the largest gains, and the best- performing students seeing declines in performance.

kp.k: Detection limits and contextual originality complicate academic policies
kp.d: Villasenor argues that unreliable AI-text detection makes bans unjust because of false accusations, and expects this problem to persist as both detection and generation improve. He presents disclosure mandates and non-mandates as possible institutional choices, while noting that clients may require disclosure in practice. He rejects treating all AI output as automatically plagiarized and distinguishes academic demands for original ideas and wording from routine reuse of proven language in motions and transactional documents, without dispensing with accuracy, argument quality or proper citation.
qs: As there is currently no sufficiently reliable way to identify text created by generative AI, law schools that attempt to enforce a ban would inevitably falsely accuse some students of using AI even when they did not.
One approach is for law schools to mandate that students disclose the fact of its use and the manner in which they used it.

Law schools should help students view and use generative AI with full contextual awareness—i.e., that for academic writing, originality is foundational, while for many other types of documents written by attorneys, including court filings and contracts, it is often far less important.
On the contrary, a practitioner needs to ensure that documents are rigorously written, strongly argued (when an argument is at issue), and properly cited.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Villasenor predicts substantial but gradual changes to legal writing, service delivery, competition and education, primarily through augmentation rather than replacement of lawyers.
pts.d: Villasenor argues that generative AI differs from earlier search and storage technologies because it contributes directly to articulating arguments. He predicts faster research and drafting across motions, contracts, regulatory filings, wills and other documents. His future motion-drafting scenario retains lawyers' responsibility for identifying the strongest arguments, supplying relevant materials and reviewing drafts; AI could generate alternative drafts, refine prose, add citations, identify rebuttals and detect inconsistencies. He anticipates fewer hallucinations and automated citation and factual checks, while still requiring human fact checking. He predicts that multilingual, interactive tools could help tenants prepare claims themselves, and that customized or hybrid tools could expand the capacity of legal-services organizations. Firms that fail to adopt effective tools would eventually face higher relative delivery costs; early vendors are not assured lasting market leadership. Graduates proficient in AI would work more efficiently and become stronger employment candidates. He expects better tools and greater user skill to improve written work, and argues for responsible curricular integration rather than bans. He also predicts that AI-detection false positives will remain a problem. These changes do not, in his account, eliminate lawyers' advantages in detailed case analysis, strategy, relationships, advocacy and mentoring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article combines cited empirical research, legal and market examples, historical analogies and explicitly hypothetical future workflows; it does not report its own productivity experiment.
pts.d: For efficiency, Villasenor cites Choi, Monahan and Schwarcz's randomized trial reporting large, consistent speed gains but only slight, inconsistent improvements in legal-analysis quality. For education, he cites Choi and Schwarcz's study finding consistent benefits only on simple multiple-choice questions, with the weakest students gaining most and the strongest declining; his explanation that experience and improved tools will overcome these limitations is an expectation, not that study's demonstrated result. For unmet need, he uses the Legal Services Corporation's 2022 Justice Gap Survey, based on a 2021 survey: 74% of low-income households experienced at least one civil legal problem, and 55% of low-income Americans personally experiencing a problem reported substantial effects on their lives. These data establish need, not generative AI's success in meeting it. He cites tenant-harassment ordinances and filing procedures to ground the proposed applications. Ye and colleagues' tenant-risk identification example concerns machine learning, not demonstrated generative-AI document preparation. LegalZoom litigation supplies an analogy for expected unauthorized-practice challenges. Announced CoCounsel adoption and Lexis+ AI student access establish early availability rather than measured benefits. Internet, search and smartphone histories support his expectations about usability, maturation and shifting market leadership. Motion-drafting time savings, future hallucination reductions and expanded service capacity are projections rather than measured results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Villasenor distinguishes early benefits from a years-to-decades evolution, making adoption and service expansion conditional on quality, usability, human oversight and regulatory accommodation.
pts.d: Writing in 2024, Villasenor places some efficiency benefits in the present for early adopters, broader changes over coming years, and technological evolution over decades. His motion scenario explicitly considers technology five, ten or fifteen years ahead, not present-day push-button court filings. Even then, drafts would require fact checking and editing, and attorneys would supply core arguments and case judgment. Access-to-justice tools are described as technically within reach, but widespread deployment would take years of development, testing, litigation and regulatory adjustment. Deployment must protect privacy and privilege, meet quality requirements and preserve consumer protection; premature release could damage users and discourage later adoption. Broad professional adoption depends on ease of use, manageable training costs, confidentiality and vendor durability. Early products may be expensive, become obsolete or disappear. His expectation of improved student writing is conditional on better tools and more skilled users. His longer horizon includes the 2030s vendor market and careers of mid-2020s graduates extending into the 2070s. He expressly cautions that interactions with other technologies make prediction uncertain.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects encompass practicing lawyers, competing firms, underserved individuals, legal-services staff, students, schools, vendors and courts, with distinct benefits and responsibilities.
pts.d: Litigators and other drafting-intensive practitioners could spend less time producing text while retaining responsibility for accuracy, persuasive reasoning and client strategy. Firms would balance efficiency and competitive costs against purchasing, training, confidentiality and market-transition risks; Villasenor suggests evaluation committees for large firms. Clients would encounter changed expectations and could impose tool-use or disclosure requirements, but the article does not quantify fee reductions or job losses. Low-income tenants and pro se litigants could obtain multilingual assistance with harassment claims; city agencies and private legal-services organizations could serve more people through staff-assisted or hybrid workflows. In this context, 'in-house' tools are tools within those organizations, not corporate legal departments. Courts and litigants could be harmed by low-quality filings if deployment is premature, while providers of self-help systems could face unauthorized-practice litigation. Students and graduates could gain efficiency and employment advantages, but remain accountable for submitted work, citation verification and appropriate attribution. Schools face curricular and procurement decisions, including vendors' incentives to acquire student testing data and institutional prestige. Lawyers' client relationships, mentoring and strategic judgment remain human-centered in the author's account.
